previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 72-year-old woman, status post orthotopic liver transplant for end-stage liver disease due to hepatitis C, was readmitted from rehabilitation with asymptomatic hyperkalemia (potassium 7.2) secondary to dehydration. She was treated in the emergency department with insulin, calcium gluconate, and Kayexalate, with potassium normalizing to 3.8 within 24 hours. Tube feedings were adjusted to a more dilute formula and increased rate to improve hydration. Her immunosuppressant was transitioned from tacrolimus to sirolimus due to low levels and persistent tremors. Liver function tests showed improvement, and diabetes was stable without insulin requirement during admission. She remained asymptomatic throughout, with stable vital signs and no complications. She was transferred back to rehabilitation on day two with a plan to continue monitoring tremors, nutrition, and medication adherence.

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  ___ female with mild elevation in LFTs, status post liver
transplant, hepatitis C cirrhosis after initiation of antibiotics, assess for
obstruction.

COMPARISON:  Abdomen ultrasound ___ and Doppler ultrasound ___.

FINDINGS:  The hepatic architecture is unremarkable in appearance.  No focal
liver lesion is identified.  No biliary dilatation is seen.  No ascites is
seen in the abdomen.  The spleen is unremarkable, measuring 10.9 cm.  No
hydronephrosis is seen on limited views of the kidneys.

Doppler examination:  Color Doppler, and spectral waveform analysis was
performed.  The main portal vein is patent with hepatopetal flow, however
Doppler velocities have changed since the prior ultrasound.  Velocity within
the main portal vein measures 26 cm/sec proximal to the anastomosis.  Just
distal to the anastomosis the velocity is increased to 151 cm/second.  This
change in velocity suggests a stenosis at the level of the anastomosis.  An
echogenic linear structure within the portal vein is seen at the anastomosis
(image #11) which could represent suture line narrowing.  The right and left
portal veins are patent with hepatopetal flow.  Appropriate arterial waveforms
are seen in the main, right and left hepatic arteries with resistive indices
of 0.83, 0.72, and 0.75 respectively.  The hepatic veins and IVC are patent.

IMPRESSION:  1. Change in velocities of the Main Portal Vein suggesting a
possible portal vein stenosis at the anastamosis.  A CTA could be performed to
further evaluate.  The remainder of the hepatic vessels are patent.

2. No biliary dilatation, no focal liver lesion, and no ascites identified.

Findings of possible portal vein stenosis were discovered at 16:00 and were
conveyed by telephone to Dr. ___ at 16:15 on ___.

EXAM:  CT angiogram of the abdomen.

CLINICAL INDICATION:  ___ woman with history of liver transplant ___
years ago, presenting with ultrasound findings suggestive of anastomotic
stenosis at the main portal vein.  Evaluation of this anastomosis.

TECHNIQUE:  Multiaxial CT images through the abdomen were obtained without and
following administration of IV contrast.  Coronal and sagittal reformatted
images were also provided for interpretation.

COMPARISON:  CT angiogram from ___, as well as ultrasound from
___.

FINDINGS:  The visualized chest demonstrates normal lungs, pleura and
heart/mediastinal structures.

No significant change in size or appearance of the transplanted liver. 
Minimal periportal edema is seen.  There is focal area of stenosis
(approximately ___ on axial images) at the main portal venous anastomosis. 
However, there is adequate perfusion and flow within the pre-anastomotic,
anastomotic and post-anastomotic portal vein.  The hepatic veins and biliary
system are grossly within normal limits.  The gallbladder is surgically
absent.  

The adrenal glands, kidneys, spleen, and bowel appear normal.  The pancreas is
moderately atrophic, but grossly unremarkable.  There is diffuse vascular
calcification involving the aorta and its branch vessels.  No evidence of free
air or ascites.  Copious amount of stool within the colon.

Mild multilevel degenerative disease involving the lower lumbar spine is
present.


IMPRESSION:  Focal (approximately up to 50%) stenosis involving the main
portal vein at the area of anastomosis.  However, there is flow proximal,
through, and distal to the area of stenosis.  Rest of the visualized liver
transplant appears well perfused.

INDICATION:  Hepatitis C cirrhosis, ___ status post liver transplant in ___
with up-trending transaminitis, concerned about rejection due to lower
tacrolimus levels on admission.  Please perform liver biopsy with rush
pathologic process and to evaluate for rejection.

PROCEDURE:  The risks and benefits of the procedure were explained to the
patient, and written informed consent was obtained.  A preprocedure timeout
was performed verifying the identity of the patient using three patient
identifiers, and the nature of the procedure to be performed.  The skin of the
right upper quadrant was prepped and draped in standard sterile fashion. 
Local anesthesia was achieved via subcutaneous injection of 6 cc of 1%
lidocaine buffered with bicarbonate.  Under direct ultrasonographic guidance,
an 18-gauge core biopsy needle was advanced into the right hepatic lobe and a
single core biopsy sample was obtained.  The sample was submitted for rush
pathologic processing as requested by the clinical team.  The patient
tolerated the procedure well, with no complications evident at the time of the
procedure.  The attending radiologist, Dr. ___ the procedure.

MODERATE SEDATION:  Moderate sedation was provided by administering 1 mg of
Versed and 50 mcg of fentanyl in divided doses intravenously throughout the
total intraservice time of 10 minutes, during which time the patient's
hemodynamic parameters were continuously monitored by radiology department
nursing staff.

IMPRESSION:
Technically successful ultrasound-guided non-targeted liver biopsy.  Sample
sent for rush pathologic analysis.

INDICATION:  ___ woman with history of hep C cirrhosis, ___ status
post liver transplant, portal vein stenosis.  Please evaluate portal vein
stenosis.

PHYSICIANS:  Dr. ___ (radiology fellow), Dr. ___
___ (radiology attending) and Dr. ___ (radiology attending) who
were present and supervised throughout the procedure.

RADIATION:  169 mGy, 16.3 minutes of fluoroscopy time.

CONTRAST:  143 mL Optiray 320.

MEDICATION:  The procedure was performed under general anesthesia.  Please see
the dedicated note for further details.  In addition, the patient received 40
mg of gentamicin IV prior to the procedure.

PROCEDURES:
1.  Right transhepatic portal venous access.
2.  Portal venography.
3.  Pressure measurements pre  and post venoplasty.
4.  Venoplasty with 10-mm, 12-mm and 14-mm balloons.

PROCEDURE DETAILS:

Following discussion of the risks, benefits and alternatives to the procedure,
informed written patient consent was obtained.  The patient was brought to the
angiographic suite and placed supine on the table.  A preprocedure timeout was
performed using three patient identifiers.  General anesthesia was induced on
the table.  

The skin of the abdomen was prepped and draped in usual sterile fashion. 
Using ultrasound guidance, a 21G Cook needle was advanced into a peripheral
portal vein radicle.  Position within the vessel was confirmed by injection of
a small amount of contrast.  Once this had been achieved, a nitinol wire was
advanced via the needle into the portal veins and passed centrally.  The wire
did not fall readily pass into the main portal vein, but rather crossed from
the right to the left main portal vein.  The needle was exchanged for an
AccuStick system.  Once better access had been obtained through the sheath of
the AccuStick system, the nitinol wire was exchanged for a stiff Glidewire. 
Despite multiple attempts, we were unable to manipulate this into the main
portal vein and the AccuStick sheath was exchanged for a 6 ___ ___ Tip
sheath.  Once this had been placed within the right main portal vein, the
combination of a stiff glide and Kumpe catheter was manipulated into the main
portal vein.  Kumpe was removed and pressure readings were obtained from the
side arm of the sheath to estimate the pressure within the right portal vein,
this measured 14 mmHg.  A straight flush catheter was then advanced over the
wire into the main portal vein and repeat measurements were obtained. 
Pressure measurements in the main portal vein were 9 mmHg, indicating a
pressure gradient of 4 mmHg.  

The straight catheter was left in the main portal vein and a venographic run
was performed. This demonstrated an approximately 50% caliber change at the
level of the anastomosis. Given the imaging findings and the pressure
gradient, we elected to perform balloon dilatation.  Serial balloon dilatation
with 10-mm, 12-mm, and 14-mm balloons was performed.  At each inflation, a
waist was evident which resolved with further inflation.  Following completion
of this maneuver, repeat pressure measurements demonstrated a main portal
venous pressure of 12 mmHg and a right portal venous pressure of 12 mmHg , ie
resolution of the gradient.
An additional portal venography was performed which demonstrated an
improvement in the appearance of the stenosis, but with a residual caliber
change.  We repeated the pressure measurements which remained equal in the
right portal and main portal vein.  Given this good result in response to
angioplasty, we elected not to place a metallic stent at this time.  The
catheter and wire were removed.  The sheath was gradually withdrawn and the
intraparenchymal portion of the access tract was embolized using Gelfoam
pledgets.  
There were no immediate post-procedure complications.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Approximately 50% caliber change at the level of the portal venous
anastomosis.
2.  Balloon venoplasty up to 14 mm.
3.  Pre-venoplasty gradient of 4 mmHg within the portal vein, post-venoplasty
the gradient resolved completely (0 mmHg) but some residual caliber change was
noted on the post plasty venogram.
